findings.statement: Fault inception: a single blue-phase-to-earth fault on one Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV circuit, about 4.5 km from Wymondley Main.
Three almost simultaneous lightning strikes were recorded next to the circuit at the Wymondley end at the time of the fault; the largest was 33.7 kA.
Lightning as the cause of the fault is well supported by agreement in time and location. It is an attribution, not a direct observation: each strike location carries an uncertainty radius.
The Wymondley end opened at 70 ms and the Eaton Socon end at 74 ms after inception, within the 80 ms Grid Code requirement at 400 kV.
The circuit was re-energised by delayed auto-reclose about 20 s after the fault.
Substation data collection and a line inspection on 10 August found no defects; voltages stayed above the fault ride-through profile.
Hornsea One's active power fell from 799 MW to 62 MW, a loss of 737 MW. Hornsea 1B and 1C de-loaded to 0 MW between 15:52:33.728Z and 15:52:33.835Z (16:52:33 BST).

The Hornsea de-load is attributed to the offshore turbine controllers responding to an insufficiently damped sub-synchronous resonance triggered by the fault. The weak internal configuration (one SGT and one OTSUA circuit on outage) contributed. The DRC worked as designed.

A damped oscillatory reactive-power response to a 2% voltage step occurred about 10 minutes before the event without de-loading, and voltage-control issues had already been identified in pre-event modelling.

Little Barford's steam turbine ST1C (244 MW) tripped because of a discrepancy between its three speed signals after fault clearance; its breaker opened 1.185 s after the SOE datum T (about 16:52:35.2 BST ±0.5 s).
GT1A (210 MW) tripped automatically on a steam bypass high-pressure excursion; its breaker opened 56.435 s after the steam turbine breaker (about 16:53:31.6 BST ±0.5 s).
GT1B (187 MW) was tripped manually for excessive steam pressure 26.993 s after GT1A (about 16:53:58.6 BST); the station's total loss was 641 MW.
Before the event (16:40:00–16:52:33) frequency stayed between 49.917 and 50.077 Hz.
Frequency fell from 49.995 Hz at 16:52:33 to 49.921 Hz at 16:52:34 and 49.77 Hz at 16:52:35. The largest 1 s fall was 0.151 Hz, consistent with about 981 MW (737 + 244) lost in about 1.2 s.
After the initial fall, frequency levelled off at about 49.08–49.27 Hz between about 16:52:50 and 16:53:30.
A second decline began at about 16:53:30–16:53:33, matching the estimated GT1A trip time; this links the second fall to the GT1A loss.
The lowest frequency was 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49, the only sample below 48.8 Hz.
Frequency recovered to 49.5 Hz at 16:55:00, 49.8 Hz at 16:56:21 and 50.0 Hz at 16:57:16.
Unknown: the root cause of the steam turbine speed-sensor discrepancy has not been established. Ofgem's link to the network fault is only a preliminary view.
Unknown: the root cause of the high steam bypass pressure that led to both gas turbine trips.
The UPS changeover to battery caused by the disturbance remains an unconfirmed operator hypothesis; the UPS units are reported as functioning correctly.
Unknown: what halted the fall at 16:53:49 and drove the recovery. The records contain no demand-disconnection, embedded-generation or reserve data, and GT1B tripped while frequency was rising.

Timing limitations: the Little Barford datum is ±0.5 s and not yet aligned with the ESO clock; the source clock labels are inferred; the two Blyth–Eccles–Stella West trip times (16:50:44 vs 16:43:25) conflict and are unresolved.

report.executive_summary:
The disturbance started with a single-phase (blue) to earth fault on one Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main 400 kV circuit at 16:52:33.490 BST [F01]. Lightning detection put three near-simultaneous strikes next to the circuit at the Wymondley end at the same moment, the largest at 33.7 kA [F02]. NGET says it is confident lightning caused the fault. That conclusion rests on strike timing and location, and the records say each strike plotted has a radius of uncertainty [F03]. Protection cleared the fault in 70 ms and 74 ms, within the 80 ms Grid Code limit [F04]. Delayed auto-reclose put the circuit back into service about 20 s later [F05]. Inspections found no defects [F06].

Two large generators then reacted to the voltage disturbance. Hornsea One's export fell from 799 MW to 62 MW, a loss of 737 MW, as Hornsea 1B and 1C de-loaded between 33.728 and 33.835 s past 16:52 [F07]. The operator and Ofgem put this down to the offshore turbine controllers responding to an insufficiently damped sub-synchronous resonance, made worse by a weak internal network configuration [F08]. A similar oscillation about 10 minutes earlier had not caused de-loading [F09]. At Little Barford the steam turbine tripped within about 1 s (244 MW) after its speed signals disagreed [F10]. The two gas turbines followed. GT1A tripped automatically about 57 s after the steam turbine (210 MW). GT1B was tripped by hand about 27 s after that (187 MW), so the station lost 641 MW in total [F11, F12].

The measured 1-second frequency record matches this sequence [F13–F18]. Frequency had been between 49.917 and 50.077 Hz. It fell from 49.995 Hz at 16:52:33 to 49.921 Hz at 16:52:34. The steepest 1 s drop was 0.151 Hz, and frequency fell below 49.8 Hz by 16:52:35. It then levelled off at about 49.1–49.27 Hz. A second decline started at about 16:53:30, close to the estimated time of the GT1A trip. Frequency reached its lowest value of 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49, which is the only sample below 48.8 Hz. It recovered to 50.0 Hz by 16:57:16.

Some questions remain open [F19–F23]. These include the root causes of the steam turbine speed-signal discrepancy and of the high steam pressures, and the UPS changeover, which is still only a hypothesis. The evidence also does not explain why frequency turned upwards after 16:53:49: no record of demand disconnection or other generation loss is included. Timing comparisons carry several uncertainties: the Little Barford time datum (±0.5 s), the unlabelled clocks in the source documents, and the conflicting times given for the Blyth trip.

sections.body: Lightning-associated single-phase fault on the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit, cleared within Grid Code limits and reclosed [F01, F02, F03, F04, F05, F06].

sections.body: Hornsea One lost 737 MW within about 350 ms of the fault [F07, F08, F09]. Little Barford's steam turbine tripped within about 1 s, followed by GT1A and GT1B, for a station loss of 641 MW [F10, F11, F12].
